summary: A survey of New-Protocol Telnet servers from September 1974. It is a status snapshot updating RFC 701, and it is itself updated by RFC 669.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the September 1974 progress check on which ARPANET computers had finished the new Telnet and which had not. It counts them and lists a few features each one supports.

questions: which telnet options were implemented in 1974
subtitle: A September 1974 headcount of which ARPANET hosts ran the new Telnet protocol and which options they supported.

tldr.problem: The network was moving from the old Telnet protocol to a new one, and people needed to know which server hosts had made the change.
tldr.mechanism: A surveying program run at various times, plus a few manual checks, tested each server from the new-protocol user Telnet at BBNA as of 23 September 1974 and tabulated the results.
tldr.outcome: Of 34 server hosts, 13 (38%) had a new-protocol server and 21 (62%) did not, so there was still a long way to go to 100% implementation.

today: RFC 702 is a point-in-time survey. The unit metadata lists RFC 701 as updated by it and RFC 669 as an update to it, and its figures describe September 1974 only.

sections.title: Changes Since Last Month
sections.content:
The previous survey produced a gratifying amount of feedback clarifying the status of several sites, but there were very few changes in the status of the host servers. The changes are listed in numerical order, with host numbers in octal.

UCLA-NMC is no longer a server. Host 205 is now BBN-TENEXD, and a new system, BBNB, is now host 61. SDC-LAB was temporarily taken off the list until it returns to the network. I4-TENEXA (117) is not a server, while KI4B-TENEX (217) is and has been added. AMES-67 fixed a bug that revealed a new-protocol server, with no options, that had been there all along. ISI-DEVTENEX (226) and USC-ECL (327) were added.
sections.plainLanguage: First comes a short list of who joined, who left and who fixed something since the previous check.

sections.title: The Tally
sections.content:
The summary counts 34 total server hosts. Of these, 21 (62%) have no new-protocol server and 13 (38%) have a new-protocol implementation. Within the 13, six run the new protocol on socket 27 with the old one on socket 1, six run it on both socket 1 and socket 27, and one runs it on socket 1 only.

The six old-on-1, new-on-27 sites are the ones whose operation is 100 percent correct as the author understands the protocol and conventions. Some servers shown as new-protocol on socket 1 actually try to talk to both old and new user Telnets, depending on which control sequences they receive. The RFC notes a minor bug in SU-AI's server, which seems to send an improper response to a request for option 0.
sections.plainLanguage: About one in three computers had the new version ready; the rest were still on the old one. A few were mixed, and one had a small slip.

sections.title: Reading the Server Table
sections.content:
The tabulation lists each host number and name, its status on socket 1 and socket 27, and the new-protocol options implemented. X means no server at that socket. An I# entry means option # is implemented incoming to the user, so the server says WILL #, and an O# entry means it is implemented outgoing from the user, so the server says DO #.

The options implemented by anyone are 0 (TRANSMIT-BINARY), 1 (ECHO), 3 (SUPPRESS-GO-AHEAD) and 6 (TIMING-MARK). Hosts such as BBN-TENEX list I1, 3, 6; O3, while AMES-67 and MIT-MULTICS list no options.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a report card with a row per computer and a few letters and numbers telling which extra features each one knows.
